items.title: [Authlib] Authlib RFC 7592 examples omit registration-access-token client binding
items.summary: DescriptionSummaryRFC 7592 (OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Protocol) lets a previously registered client read, update, or delete its own registration, authenticated by a registration_access_token issued specifically to that client at registration time. The entire security model of this protocol depends on the server verifying that the token presented in the request actually belongs to the client identified in the request, not merely that the token is valid for some client.Authlib's ClientConfigurationEndpoint implements the control flow correctly in structure, calling authenticate_token, then authenticate_client, then check_permission, and treats all three as abstract methods that "Developers MUST implement in subclass." The problem is that the documented example implementations for these methods, taken together exactly as written, never perform the one check that matters: binding the authenticated token to the specific client being accessed. A developer who implements these methods by following the provided examples ends up with a complete authorization bypass on this endpoint.Detailsauthenticate_client's documented example (authlib/oauth2/rfc7592/endpoint.py):def authenticate_client(self, request):    """Read a client from the request payload.    Developers MUST implement this method in subclass::        def authenticate_client(self, request):            client_id = request.payload.data.get("client_id")            return Client.get(client_id=client_id)    :return: client instance    """    raise NotImplementedError()This looks the target client up purely by the client_id supplied in the request payload, with no reference to the token at all.check_permission's documented example, in the same file:def check_permission(self, client, request):    """Checks whether the current client is allowed to be accessed, edited    or deleted. Developers MUST implement it in subclass, e.g.::        def check_permission(self, client, request):            return client.editable    :return: boolean    """    raise NotImplementedError()This checks a property of the target client alone (whether it is generally "editable"), again with no reference to request.credential, the authenticated token object returned earlier by authenticate_token and stored on the request specifically so that later steps can check it:def create_configuration_response(self, request):    token = self.authenticate_token(request)    if not token:        raise AccessDeniedError()    request.credential = token    client = self.authenticate_client(request)    ...    if not self.check_permission(client, request):        raise UnauthorizedClientError(...)request.credential is set specifically so that a binding check can be performed downstream, but neither documented example ever reads it. Following both examples as written produces an implementation where the only requirements to access, modify, or delete a client's registration are: possessing any valid registration_access_token for any client, and knowing or guessing the target client_id.This is meaningfully different from how the equivalent example is written for the token introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) elsewhere in the same codebase, which does correctly demonstrate checking the authenticated caller's own identity (authlib/oauth2/rfc7662/introspection.py):def check_permission(self, token, client, request):    """Check if the request has permission to introspect the token. Developers    MUST implement this method::        def check_permission(self, token, client, request):            # only allow a special client to introspect the token            return client.client_id == "introspection_client"    """In that endpoint, client represents the already-authenticated caller (verified through normal client credential authentication earlier in the flow), so checking a property of client is meaningful authorization logic. In the RFC 7592 endpoint, client instead represents the target being acted upon, not the caller, so the same style of example is actively misleading: it looks like a reasonable authorization check but performs none of the binding the protocol requires.No file anywhere in the repository, including the Flask, Django, and SQLAlchemy integration modules, provides a complete, corrected reference implementation of ClientConfigurationEndpoint. The misleading docstring examples are the only guidance shipped for this endpoint.Realistic exploitabilityRFC 7591 dynamic client registration is commonly deployed without requiring an initial access token, since the specification explicitly anticipates open, self-service registration as a normal deployment model. Under that common configuration, an attacker can freely self-register their own throwaway client with no authentication at all, receive a valid registration_access_token scoped to that throwaway client, and then present that same token against /register/{target_client_id} for any other client, since neither documented example checks

items.title: [pyasn1] pyasn1 has quadratic CPU consumption in constructed BIT STRING decoding
items.summary: SummaryIn pyasn1 through 0.6.4, decoding a constructed BIT STRING with many fragments repeatedly shifts and copies the entire value accumulated so far. For fixed-size fragments, CPU time grows quadratically with the encoded input size. An application that passes sufficiently large, attacker-controlled ASN.1 data to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion during decode(); no conversion or formatting of the decoded value is required.The BER and CER decoders reach this path for constructed BIT STRING values, with or without an asn1Spec. The DER decoder rejects constructed BIT STRING in schema-less decoding, but its schema-driven path accepts a definite-length constructed BIT STRING when given a matching asn1Spec and reaches the same vulnerable code. Constructed BIT STRING is not valid DER; this DER exposure is due to decoder permissiveness. DER rejects the indefinite-length form.This is a separate decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER accumulation fixed in CVE-2026-59885.Technical detailsIn the 0.6.4 BitStringPayloadDecoder, both the definite-length and indefinite-length fragment loops call BitString.fromOctetString(..., prepend=bitString) for every fragment. fromOctetString shifts the growing SizedInteger left by the fragment's bit length and ORs in the fragment. Shifting an ever-larger Python integer for each fixed-size fragment makes total work O(n²) for n fragments. The fragments are siblings, so the decoder's nesting-depth limit does not constrain their count; its limit on the number of length octets does not prevent the demonstrated inputs.In 0.6.4, DER's tag-driven map disables constructed BIT STRING, while its schema-driven type map retains the inherited decoder that permits it. This explains why a schema-less DER rejection is not a negative result for all DER decoding.Under X.690, a conforming CER constructed BIT STRING uses an indefinite-length outer encoding and primitive fragments with 1000 contents octets except possibly the last. That form reaches the affected indefinite-length loop. DER requires primitive string encoding, although the schema-driven pyasn1 decoder accepts the definite-length constructed example below.ImpactAn application is exposed when untrusted input can reach one of the affected decoder paths and its input limits admit enough fragments. The work occupies the decoding thread or worker and may cause denial of service. Whether the input is network-accessible or unauthenticated depends on the calling application. This advisory makes no claim that every application using pyasn1, or any particular protocol implementation, accepts such input.Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER values trigger the issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted values could occupy a finite decoder-worker pool and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not claim that every application is network-exposed or fully unavailable; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See FIRST's library-scoring guidance.ReproducerThe definite-length example below is valid BER. It is deliberately not a conforming CER or DER encoding. The second constructor uses conforming CER fragment sizing and framing. CPU times are machine-dependent; run the larger cases only in a local test environment.import timefrom pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as ber_decoderfrom pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cer_decoderfrom pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as der_decoderfrom pyasn1.error import PyAsn1Errorfrom pyasn1.type import univdef encode_length(size):    octets = size.to_bytes((size.bit_length() + 7) // 8, "big")    return bytes((0x80 | len(octets),)) + octetsdef definite_fragments(count):    body = b"\x03\x02\x00\xa5" * count  # one data octet per BIT STRING fragment    return b"\x23" + encode_length(len(body)) + bodydef cer_fragments(count):    # Each primitive fragment has 1000 contents octets: one unused-bits    # octet (zero) followed by 999 data octets.    fragment = b"\x03" + encode_length(1000) + b"\x00" + b"\xa5" * 999    return b"\x23\x80" + fragment * count + b"\x00\x00"def measure(label, decode, payload, **options):    start = time.process_time()    value, remainder = decode(payload, **options)    print(label, len(payload), f"{time.process_time() - start:.3f}s CPU")    assert not remainder and len(value) > 0for count in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):    measure(f"BER {count} fragments", ber_decoder.decode,            definite_fragments(count))for count in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000):    measure(f"CER {count} fragments", cer_decoder.decode,            cer_fragments(count))sample = definite_fragments(1_000)measure("DER with BIT STRING schema", der_decoder.decode, sample,        asn1Spec=univ.BitString())try:    der_

items.title: [pyasn1] pyasn1 has quadratic-complexity denial of service in binary REAL decoding
items.summary: SummaryIn pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a binary-encoded ASN.1 REAL with a large mantissa can consume CPU time quadratic in the mantissa length. The BER, CER, and DER decoders all use the affected RealPayloadDecoder. An application is exposed when it passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 containing a REAL value to one of these decoders, either without an asn1Spec or with a schema that includes REAL. The work occurs inside decode(); the application does not need to convert, print, or otherwise use the resulting REAL object.This is distinct from CVE-2026-59886, which concerns converting an already-decoded REAL to a Python float. That issue was fixed in 0.6.4 and its advisory states that decoding alone does not trigger it.Root cause and affected componentsFor binary REAL values, RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder in v0.6.4 builds the mantissa one octet at a time:p = 0while chunk:    p <<= 8    p |= chunk[0]    chunk = chunk[1:]Each shift processes an integer that grows with the mantissa; with byte strings, each slice also copies the remaining suffix. Repeating both operations for every octet makes decoding quadratic in mantissa size. The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit does not impose a practical mantissa-size limit for the inputs demonstrated below. CER and DER reuse the BER REAL payload decoder, so all three paths reach this loop.The vulnerable loop is present in every available repository release tag inspected, from v0.2.1 through v0.6.4. Runtime measurements below were made on v0.6.4; older releases were checked for the loop, not benchmarked individually.ImpactA comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoder worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer. The attacker must be able to supply data that the application sends to an affected decoder, and application-level input limits may reduce exposure. The demonstrated effect is CPU exhaustion during decoding; this advisory does not assert a network endpoint, unauthenticated access, or an affected downstream application by itself.Reproduction and evidenceThe following example uses pyasn1 0.6.4. The 0x09 tag identifies REAL; 0x80 0x00 selects a positive, base-2 binary value with a one-octet zero exponent, followed by a large mantissa. It exercises decode() only.import timefrom pyasn1.codec.ber import decoder as berfrom pyasn1.codec.cer import decoder as cerfrom pyasn1.codec.der import decoder as derdef real_value(mantissa_octets):    content = b"\x80\x00" + b"\xff" * mantissa_octets    length = len(content).to_bytes(3, "big")    return b"\x09\x83" + length + contentfor codec in (ber, cer, der):    for size in (50_000, 100_000, 200_000):        substrate = real_value(size)        started = time.process_time()        value, rest = codec.decode(substrate)        print(codec.__name__, size, time.process_time() - started)        assert not rest        assert tuple(value)[1:] == (2, 0)The original report measured the following BER CPU times on repository commit aa05757. That commit is later than the official v0.6.4 tag; the vulnerable loop is identical in the tagged release.Mantissa sizeReporter's BER CPU time50,000 octets0.328 s100,000 octets1.299 s200,000 octets6.043 s400,000 octets24.095 sThe same report measured 5.645 s for a 200,000-octet mantissa through DER.A separate local reproduction on the official v0.6.4 tag (d43496f, CPython 3.14.8, macOS arm64) measured BER at 0.209 s, 0.884 s, and 3.451 s for 50,000, 100,000, and 200,000 mantissa octets respectively. CER and DER each took about 0.89 s at 100,000 octets. These are machine-specific measurements; the repeated near-fourfold cost for doubled input is the relevant result. Neither reproduction calls float(), str(), or prettyPrint().Fixpyasn1 0.6.5 replaces the per-octet shift and slice loop with one int.from_bytes(bytes(chunk), "big") conversion. Sign, scale, exponent, and the decoded REAL tuple are preserved. The fix is in the shared BER payload decoder and therefore covers BER, CER, and DER. A local check of the 0.6.5 candidate decoded a 200,000-octet mantissa correctly through all three codecs; the check does not establish behavior for every application using REAL.WorkaroundsUpgrade to pyasn1 0.6.5. Until then, reject or strictly limit attacker-controlled ASN.1 input that may contain REAL values before passing it to pyasn1. The appropriate size limit depends on the application's available CPU time and request volume.Referenceshttps://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/security/advisories/GHSA-mm57-4v3p-rchxhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119197https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/pull/132https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/commit/ce3ec3390784780a530047e0e77be5ff457636a4https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/releases/tag/v0.6.5https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mm57-4v3p-rchx

items.title: [pyasn1] pyasn1 has quadratic-time denial of service in constructed string and indefinite-length ANY decoding
items.summary: SummaryIn pyasn1 0.6.4 and earlier, decoding a constructed OCTET STRING or character string made of many fragments can spend disproportionate CPU time repeatedly copying the accumulated value. A separate indefinite-length ANY path has the same problem while collecting the encoded components. The work grows roughly quadratically with the number of fixed-size fragments, although the input and decoded value grow linearly. An application that lets an attacker supply such ASN.1 input to an affected decoder can suffer CPU exhaustion.The affected string paths are available in BER and CER. The DER decoder also accepts certain non-DER constructed strings: a definite-length constructed OCTET STRING when an asn1Spec selects univ.OctetString, and constructed character strings such as UTF8String even without a schema. Indefinite-length ANY is affected in BER and CER when an asn1Spec selects univ.Any; DER rejects indefinite lengths.This is a distinct decoder path from the OBJECT IDENTIFIER/RELATIVE-OID accumulation addressed by CVE-2026-59885. It has the same complexity class, but the OID fix in 0.6.4 did not change these string or ANY loops.Technical detailsIn the v0.6.4 BER decoder, OctetStringPayloadDecoder appends each decoded fragment to a growing bytes value with header += component in both its definite-length and indefinite-length constructed forms. AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder similarly uses chunk += component. In the exercised paths, each concatenation copies an increasingly large prefix. For N fixed-size fragments, the total copied data grows with 1 + 2 + ... + N, or O(N²).The OCTET STRING decoder is also the base class of the decoders for UTF8String, NumericString, PrintableString, TeletexString, VideotexString, IA5String, GraphicString, VisibleString, GeneralString, UniversalString, BMPString, ObjectDescriptor, GeneralizedTime, and UTCTime. These types inherit the same constructed-string reassembly path.The DER decoder's OCTET STRING restriction replaces the tag-driven decoder, but its schema-driven TYPE_MAP retains the BER-derived decoder. Thus der.decode(data) rejects a constructed OCTET STRING, while der.decode(data, asn1Spec=univ.OctetString()) accepts its definite-length form and reaches the accumulation loop. DER does not replace the inherited character-string decoders, so a constructed UTF8String is also accepted without asn1Spec. These inputs violate X.690's DER string-encoding rule and should not be described as valid DER encodings.The original short-fragment, definite-length OCTET STRING reproducer is valid BER. The CER decoder accepts it, but it is not a conforming CER string encoding: X.690 requires an indefinite-length outer constructed string and 1,000 contents octets per fragment except possibly the last. A conforming CER-shaped constructed OCTET STRING with those fragment sizes also reaches the loop and shows quadratic growth. The indefinite-length ANY reproducer below can represent a CER SEQUENCE OF OCTET STRING and reaches the separate ANY loop when decoded with an ANY schema.The decoder's eight-octet length-field limit and nesting-depth limit do not bound the number of sibling fragments in these examples. The BER reproducer below uses only a three-octet outer length field; all fragments have shallow nesting. There is no per-message fragment-count cap in v0.6.4.ImpactIf an application passes attacker-controlled ASN.1 to the affected decode() or StreamingDecoder path without an adequate input or resource limit, a megabyte-scale value can occupy a decoding worker for seconds. Repeated inputs can exhaust available CPU. Whether this is reachable before authentication, or through a particular protocol, depends on the application; the library finding alone does not establish those conditions. No confidentiality or integrity impact is claimed.Severity assessment (CVSS v3.1)The 7.5 Base score assumes a reasonable application that automatically decodes attacker-supplied ASN.1 from unauthenticated network input. Valid BER and conforming CER inputs trigger the string-reassembly issue without special conditions, privileges, or user interaction. Repeated crafted inputs could occupy all available decoder workers and deny service while the attack continues. No confidentiality or integrity impact is demonstrated. This library-level score does not assert that every adopter has such an endpoint or loses all service; deployment-specific input limits and architecture may change the score. See FIRST's library-scoring guidance.On the official v0.6.4 tag, local CPU-time measurements with CPython 3.14.8 on macOS arm64 gave the following results. Times vary by machine and Python runtime; the input-size scaling is the relevant observation. “Fixed” means the local 0.6.5 decoder fix applied to the same inputs.Decoder path and inputFragmentsv0.6.4 CPUFixed CPUBER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.40 MB100,000 × 2 payload bytes0.340 s0.160 sBER constructed OCTET STRING, 0.80 MB200,000 × 2 payload bytes0.886 s0.312 sB

items.title: [pyasn1] pyasn1 has quadratic CPU use in schemaless BER/CER/DER container decoding
items.summary: SummaryWhen an application decodes attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER data without an ASN.1 schema, a container with many distinct long tag IDs can cause quadratic CPU use. Repeated inputs can exhaust CPU and reduce service availability.DetailsConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless inserts every decoded component’s TagSet into a growing set, although it only needs to distinguish one tag set from two or more. Attacker-chosen tag IDs can have colliding TagSet hashes, making each later insertion compare against an increasing number of earlier tags. This path is present in v0.6.4 and is inherited by the CER and DER decoders. The proposed fix stops growing the classification set after it contains two distinct tag sets, while retaining every decoded component and its order.  On v0.6.4 with CPython 3.12.10, increasing the collision input from 3,200 to 6,400 components raised decode CPU time from 0.438 to 1.747 seconds; a comparable control rose from 0.031 to 0.065 seconds. Both inputs decoded successfully with the expected values and an empty remainder.Proof of conceptRun this outside the repository checkout in a fresh Python 3.12 environment with pyasn1==0.6.4 installed:import sysimport timefrom pyasn1.codec.ber import decoderfrom pyasn1.type import univdef enc_tag(tag_id):    groups = [tag_id & 0x7f]    tag_id >>= 7    while tag_id:        groups.append((tag_id & 0x7f) | 0x80)        tag_id >>= 7    return b'\xbf' + bytes(reversed(groups))def payload(tag_ids):    body = b''.join(enc_tag(tag_id) + b'\x03\x04\x01A'                    for tag_id in tag_ids)    length = len(body).to_bytes((len(body).bit_length() + 7) // 8, 'big')    return b'\x30' + bytes([0x80 | len(length)]) + length + bodyfor count in (3200, 6400):    cases = (        ("collision", [32 + i * sys.hash_info.modulus                       for i in range(count)]),        ("control", [(1 << 70) + i for i in range(count)]),    )    for name, tag_ids in cases:        wire = payload(tag_ids)        start = time.process_time()        value, remainder = decoder.decode(wire)        cpu_seconds = time.process_time() - start        assert type(value) is univ.Sequence        assert len(value) == count and remainder == b''        for position, tag_id in enumerate(tag_ids):            component = value.getComponentByPosition(position)            assert component.asOctets() == b'A'            assert component.tagSet[-1].tagId == tag_id        print(count, name, len(wire), round(cpu_seconds, 3))ImpactApplications that pass attacker-controlled bytes to schemaless BER, CER, or DER decoding can spend disproportionate CPU time on a relatively small, valid input. The demonstrated impact is availability; no confidentiality or integrity impact was observed.Referenceshttps://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/security/advisories/GHSA-fm9c-5rcf-2q5phttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119194https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/pull/132https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/commit/a36e3a3d067148d26197a6b7221fd0e2cde9cc86https://github.com/pyasn1/pyasn1/releases/tag/v0.6.5https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fm9c-5rcf-2q5p

items.title: [graphql-core] GraphQL-core has denial of service via memory leak in aborted validations
items.summary: SummaryWhen a validation was aborted because the document contained more errors than allowed by max_errors (100 by default), validate() raised a single module-level ValidationAbortedError instance. Python appends the frames of every raise to the existing __traceback__ of an exception that is raised again, so every aborted validation extended the traceback of this shared error. That traceback kept the frames, and with them the document, the validation context and all errors of every aborted validation, alive for the lifetime of the process.DetailsAny client can trigger an aborted validation by sending a small document with more than 100 validation errors, e.g. 101 unknown fields. No authentication is required, and since validation runs before execution, depth limiters and complexity analyzers do not prevent it. Each such request permanently retained about 124 KiB on CPython 3.12, without an upper limit, so memory grew with every request until the process was restarted or killed.GraphQL.js uses a shared error object at the same place, but JavaScript errors capture their stack trace only once when they are created, so it is not affected. GraphQL-core 3.2 creates a new error for each aborted validation and is not affected either.Proof of conceptimport gcimport tracemallocfrom graphql import build_schema, parse, validateschema = build_schema("type Query { a: Int }")document = parse("{ " + " ".join(f"f{i}" for i in range(101)) + " }")tracemalloc.start()validate(schema, document)gc.collect()base = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0]for _ in range(200):    validate(schema, document)gc.collect()print((tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0] - base) // 1024, "KiB")With GraphQL-core 3.3.0 on CPython 3.12, the retained memory grows from 147 KiB after one call to about 25 MB after 200 calls. With the fix, it stays constant at about 180 KiB.ImpactDenial of service through memory exhaustion. A few thousand small requests are enough to push a worker past a typical 256 MB or 512 MB container limit and trigger an OOM kill. No data is disclosed or modified.PatchesFixed in 3.3.1.validate() now creates a new ValidationAbortedError for every aborted validation and removes its traceback and exception context before returning it, so that the returned errors do not keep the frames of the validation alive. The module-level validation_aborted_error instance, which was not exported, has been removed.WorkaroundsIf you cannot upgrade, clear the traceback of the shared error after each validation:from graphql.validation import validate as validate_documentfrom graphql.validation.validate import validation_aborted_errordef validate(*args, **kwargs):    try:        return validate_document(*args, **kwargs)    finally:        validation_aborted_error.__traceback__ = NonePass this function instead of the original validate where your framework allows it.CreditsReported by @riodw. @Fire162 submitted a first fix in #288.Referenceshttps://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/security/advisories/GHSA-mpqx-q82w-9x46https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119286https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/issues/287https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/pull/288https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/commit/3c319fd9f4b8f6c9db4189520561bf8dd0e70be9https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/releases/tag/v3.3.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mpqx-q82w-9x46

items.title: [oauthlib] OAuthLib: Token grants can use attacker-supplied client_id for authorization after authenticating a different client
items.summary: SummaryOAuthlib's token grant handlers can authenticate one client while authorizing the grant type and requested scopes using a different, attacker-supplied client_id from the request body.In affected token grant flows, authenticate_client(request) sets request.client to the authenticated client object, but OAuthlib does not require request.client_id to match request.client.client_id. If the request body already contains client_id=..., OAuthlib keeps that value and passes it to validate_grant_type() and validate_scopes().As a result, an authenticated low-privilege confidential client can authenticate as itself, submit another client's client_id in the token request body, and cause grant and scope validation to run under that other client identity.Affected SurfaceThe affected public surface is the OAuth2 token endpoint handling for:client_credentialspassword / Resource Owner Password CredentialsThe issue is relevant to OAuthlib provider deployments where:the attacker has credentials for one valid lower-privilege confidential client;another client has broader grants or scopes;the application validator uses the client_id argument passed by OAuthlib in validate_grant_type() or validate_scopes(), as the RequestValidator API is designed to support.Deployments whose validators ignore the client_id argument and authorize only from request.client may not be affected.DetailsRequest parses query and body parameters into request attributes, including client_id:https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/b3f9edffed6b370e3eb92721cea0da22ec7e18b9/oauthlib/common.py#L360-L397The RequestValidator.authenticate_client() contract requires the integrator to authenticate the client and set request.client:https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/b3f9edffed6b370e3eb92721cea0da22ec7e18b9/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/request_validator.py#L41-L66For the client_credentials grant, OAuthlib authenticates the client, verifies that request.client has a client_id, then performs grant and scope validation before normalizing request.client_id from request.client.client_id:https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/b3f9edffed6b370e3eb92721cea0da22ec7e18b9/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/client_credentials.py#L106-L119The problematic order is:if not self.request_validator.authenticate_client(request):    ...elif not hasattr(request.client, 'client_id'):    ...self.validate_grant_type(request)request.client_id = request.client_id or request.client.client_idself.validate_scopes(request)Because OAuthlib only fills request.client_id when it is missing, an attacker-supplied body value such as client_id=high survives even when request.client.client_id == "low".The shared grant helper then authorizes using request.client_id, while passing the authenticated client object separately:validate_grant_type(request.client_id, request.grant_type, request.client, request): https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/b3f9edffed6b370e3eb92721cea0da22ec7e18b9/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/base.py#L152-L162validate_scopes(request.client_id, request.scopes, request.client, request): https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/b3f9edffed6b370e3eb92721cea0da22ec7e18b9/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/base.py#L164-L176The same identity split exists in the Resource Owner Password Credentials flow. After client authentication and user validation, OAuthlib validates the grant and scopes before replacing a missing request.client_id from request.client.client_id:https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/b3f9edffed6b370e3eb92721cea0da22ec7e18b9/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/resource_owner_password_credentials.py#L87-L97https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/b3f9edffed6b370e3eb92721cea0da22ec7e18b9/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/resource_owner_password_credentials.py#L178-L195This creates an inconsistent identity state:request.client.client_id == "low"   # authenticated clientrequest.client_id == "high"         # attacker-supplied request parameterOAuthlib then calls application authorization hooks with both values, but uses the attacker-controlled request.client_id as the first-class client_id argument.ImpactAn authenticated lower-privilege confidential client can obtain tokens authorized under another client's grant and scope policy if the application's validator follows the RequestValidator API and authorizes by the client_id argument.Concrete impact can include:issuing access tokens with scopes not assigned to the authenticated client;allowing a low-privilege client to use a grant type reserved for a higher-privilege client;persisting tokens under a spoofed client_id while the authenticated client object is different.This is a token authorization bypass, not an unauthenticated attack. The attacker needs valid credentials for one client.PoCCreate the following files in an empty directory.requirements.txt:oauthlib==3.3.1repro.py:import base64import jsonfrom oauthlib.oauth2 import (    BearerToken,    ClientCredentialsGrant,    RequestValidator,    Resourc

items.title: [openwisp-controller] OpenWISP Controller CA CRL REST API does not scope requests to managed organizations
items.summary: SummaryThe authenticated REST API endpoint for downloading a CA Certificate Revocation List resolves the requested CA without applying the organization-scoped queryset used by the rest of the PKI API.An organization manager with CA view permission can request another organization's sequential CA ID and receive that CA's CRL. The endpoint is intended to be authenticated and organization-scoped, so it should use the same access-control path as GET /api/v1/controller/ca/<id>/.Affected endpointGET /api/v1/controller/ca/<integer-id>/crlCrlDownloadView inherits ProtectedAPIMixin, which requires an authenticated organization manager with the relevant model permission. However, retrieve() resolves the CA with get_object_or_404(Ca, pk=kwargs["pk"]). This bypasses FilterByOrganizationManaged and does not perform an object-level permission check.Consequently, a manager of organization A can enumerate CA integer IDs and retrieve the CRL for a CA belonging to organization B. The sibling CA detail endpoint is correctly organization-scoped and returns 404 for the same cross-organization request.ImpactThe endpoint returns only the CRL, including CA issuer information and revoked certificate serial numbers. It does not disclose CA private keys and does not permit modification.django-x509 exposes CRLs publicly by default unless DJANGO_X509_CRL_PROTECTED = True. Therefore, the default configuration does not gain a new confidentiality exposure from this REST API behavior. Nonetheless, the endpoint is part of the authenticated, organization-scoped REST API and does not enforce its intended authorization boundary.Deployments that explicitly protect CRLs have a stronger expectation that this endpoint will scope access to the requester's managed organizations. The practical impact is low, but the authorization behavior should be corrected for consistency and defense in depth.RemediationResolve the CA through the view's organization-scoped queryset. Set queryset = Ca.objects.all(), replace the direct get_object_or_404(Ca, pk=kwargs["pk"]) lookup with self.get_object(), and add a regression test that a same-organization manager receives 200 while a manager of another organization receives 404.Referenceshttps://github.com/openwisp/openwisp-controller/security/advisories/GHSA-9gh4-xw24-9xh5https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-116677https://github.com/openwisp/openwisp-controller/commit/90ded783267aa11b89768b0ec9ae69895cc3730chttps://github.com/openwisp/openwisp-controller/commit/9e1869e17734a0f34bc428622d463c1a8c230720https://github.com/openwisp/openwisp-controller/releases/tag/1.3.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gh4-xw24-9xh5
